segments.say: Let's leave the glowing screen on Tomas's sofa for a moment, and follow him into the hours after he puts it down. The flat is quiet. The city hums softly beyond the window. And a thought drifts up, the way thoughts do when the evening is slow. Maybe this is simply how I am. Maybe I'm just a lonely person.

It's a heavy sentence, and it's worth noticing how final it sounds. Not, I feel lonely tonight. But, I am lonely, as if it were written on a label, like his height or the color of his eyes. Tomas has said this to himself before, on other Sunday evenings. Each time it sounds a little more like a fact and a little less like a passing thought.

That is the myth we're going to look at now. It's an understandable one. When a feeling lasts, and when it returns again and again, it starts to feel like part of our personality. Nobody asks us to believe it, and nobody means any harm by it. The mind simply reaches for a tidy explanation, and a permanent label can feel strangely tidier than a feeling that comes and goes.

Here is a different picture, and it comes from the research. Think about weather and climate. Climate is the long pattern of a place. Weather is what happens on a given afternoon. Loneliness, it seems, behaves much more like weather. It can be heavy for a stretch, then lift, then return, and what you feel today says less about who you are than about what your days have been holding.

Researchers who study loneliness have asked people to keep a daily diary. In a study published in 2010, Hawkley, Preacher and Cacioppo followed adults across several days, asking how lonely they felt each evening. Loneliness showed some stability, so people had their own usual level. But the authors also described substantial day-to-day variability. The same person could feel quite different from one day to the next.

show.what: Loneliness varied a great deal from one day to the next in the same people

segments.say: That study followed two hundred and fifteen adults drawn from a population sample, with an average age of around fifty-seven. They were not patients, and they were not chosen because they were unusually lonely. They were simply people living their lives. And across those lives, the feeling rose and fell. It's a small but reassuring detail, because it suggests that loneliness is something people move through, rather than something people are.

So what makes it rise and fall? Often, quite ordinary things. A week full of plans can soften it. A weekend with no one to call can sharpen it. A move to a new city, a new job, a friend who has gone quiet, a rainy Sunday. Tomas's loneliness is probably not a fixed amount carried around inside him. It's more likely a reading that shifts with the days he is having.

These are everyday examples, not findings from one study. A kind message from someone can lighten an afternoon. A week crowded with obligations can leave no room to notice it at all. A long weekend with no plans can make it louder. And moving somewhere new can bring it in for a while. The point is only that circumstances matter, and circumstances can change.

show.title: Things that can nudge the feeling
items: A long weekend with no plans

segments.say: There's another part of this myth worth looking at gently. When someone feels lonely for a long time, they often feel low as well, and the two can seem like one big grey cloud. It's natural to ask which comes first. Does sadness make us lonely, or does loneliness make us sad? Researchers have tried to untangle that very question, and the answer is a bit surprising.

show.title: Does a low mood make it worse?

segments.say: From the inside, the two feel almost identical. A low mood makes a message feel like effort. Loneliness makes a quiet evening feel heavier. And so it's easy to believe the whole thing is one fixed, inner condition, something that belongs to us, like a coastline. But feelings that are tangled together can still be separate threads, and separate threads can be handled one at a time.

This is a study published in 2010, by Cacioppo, Hawkley and Thisted, in the journal Psychology and Aging. They followed adults over five years, tracking both loneliness and low mood. They found that loneliness predicted later depressive symptoms. But depressive symptoms did not predict later loneliness. And this held even after accounting for things like stress, social support and a naturally gloomy temperament.

show.what: Loneliness predicted later depressive symptoms, but depressive symptoms did not predict later loneliness

segments.say: The group was two hundred and twenty-nine adults, aged between fifty and sixty-eight, from a diverse community sample. That's an older group than Tomas, and these are associations measured over time, so we should hold the result lightly. But the authors' reading was that loneliness may be an early signal worth listening to, rather than just a side effect of feeling low.

show.title: Adults followed for five years
show.label: aged 50 to 68, from a diverse community sample

segments.say: There's something hopeful in that. If loneliness can come before low mood, then noticing it early, and treating it as a message, may matter more than waiting for a bigger cloud to gather. And it's a very different story from I'm just made this way. It says that the feeling responds to what's going on around us, which means that what's going on around us can respond back.

It's only a small saying, not a finding. But it fits what the researchers keep describing. A feeling can visit for a day, for a season, even for a long, hard year, and still be a visitor. Tomas has felt it on many Sundays. That doesn't make it his address. It makes it a weather system passing through a flat in the city.

show.text: A feeling that visits is not a place you live.

segments.say: Imagine Tomas's flat on a Monday morning. It's the same chair, the same window, the same folded blanket. But the light has changed, and so has the feeling in the room. Nothing about the furniture decided how Sunday evening would feel, and nothing about it decides this morning either. Rooms change with the light, and so can we, without becoming a different person.

show.cap: The same room, a different morning

segments.say: There's one more reason people take loneliness personally, and it has to do with how quickly we expect closeness to arrive. Tomas moved to this city a while ago. He's met people. He's had pleasant chats at work, and a few warm messages. And yet he hasn't found his people, and so he wonders whether something is wrong with him.

It's easy to look around and assume that everyone else simply has friends, already formed and waiting, like chairs pulled up to a table. We rarely see how long those friendships took. We only see them as they are now, comfortable and easy, and we compare that with our own early beginnings, which are always a little clumsy and slow.

So let's look at the time it actually takes. In a study published in 2019, Jeffrey Hall asked people who had recently moved and were looking for new friends how their friendships developed. He found that it took roughly fifty hours of time together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, about ninety hours to become a friend, and more than two hundred to become a close friend.

show.where: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, published 2019
show.what: About 50 hours together to become casual friends, about 90 to become friends, and more than 200 to become close friends

segments.say: Here are those three numbers side by side. Fifty hours. Ninety hours. And around two hundred or more. These are approximate figures from the study, and they will differ from person to person, so please hold them lightly. But the shape is clear. Closeness is not made in an evening. It builds, hour by hour, from a great many small moments of being together.

show.title: Hours together, roughly (close friend means 200 or more)

segments.say: If you take that seriously, Tomas's situation looks different. A few months into a new city, with a handful of pleasant conversations, he may simply be partway through a process that takes many hours. Nothing has gone wrong. The friendships he wants may only need more time together than he has had so far. And that is not a flaw in him. It's just arithmetic, and arithmetic is kind in that it doesn't judge anyone.

show.sub: Early weeks are not a verdict

segments.say: It's also worth noticing that hours are made of small pieces. A coffee, a walk, a shared task, a long laugh over something unimportant. None of those feels like a big step when it happens. But they are the building blocks. Time that looks ordinary from the inside, adds up to something very real when you look back across a year.

Let's gather a few gentle thoughts. Loneliness behaves more like weather than a fixed trait. It may be an early signal, and signals are meant to be heard. Closeness takes many hours, for nearly everyone. And the early weeks of a new place are only that, the early weeks. None of this asks Tomas to feel differently tonight. It simply gives him a more accurate and more forgiving story.

show.title: A kinder way to hold it
items: It can be a signal, not a verdict
Early weeks are only early weeks

segments.say: Tomas is still on his sofa, and the evening has gone a little dimmer. He turns the new idea over, the way you'd turn a smooth stone in your pocket.

Perhaps he is not a lonely person. Perhaps he's a person who is feeling lonely, in the middle of a long process, on a quiet Sunday. It's a very small shift in wording. It lets in a surprising amount of air, and it leaves room for the evening to turn out differently.

show.text: Not a lonely person, a person feeling lonely.

segments.say: And once you're no longer fighting a verdict, a practical question appears. If loneliness is a signal, and closeness takes time, then what actually helps? The most common answer is a simple one, and Tomas has heard it many times, from friends and from his own head. Just go out more. Get out there. Meet people. It sounds so sensible that few people stop to ask whether it's true.
